summary: This file is a bound Google-digitized volume holding three consecutive economic and political reports, not only No. 33. No. 33 (June 1948) covers the monsoon-quiet month after the Cheju and May disorders, the first full month without North Korean electricity (cut 14 May), collapsing industrial output, the new weighted wholesale price index (12-fold rise since 1945), summer grain and land sales, and the new National Assembly drafting the Constitution. No. 34 (July-August 1948) is the final SKIG report, covering passage of the Constitution, Rhee's election, the 15 August proclamation of the Republic, the end of USAMGIK, with three-year retrospectives on population, vested property, labor, utilities, public works, police, press, youth, women and culture. No. 35 (September-October 1948) is the first economic-only summation under the Republic, with transfer of offices to Korean ministries, rice collection and the ration-roll 'ghost population'. Historians get dense statistics on prices, trade, power, coal, finance and land reform.
highlights: June 1948 was the first full month without North Korean electric power: only 41 million KWH reached consumers, 15 million less than May, and flour, paper and cement output fell sharply from April.
Arthur Peterson's first weighted index showed South Korean wholesale prices rose about twelve-fold from August 1945 to July 1948, reaching 171 on a 1947 base of 100.
The new National Assembly adopted its rules 153 to 1 on 10 June and began reading the draft Constitution on 23 June, disputing presidential powers and unicameralism.
On 8 June U.S. planes bombed Dok Do fishermen, provoking Korean protest from all factions; Cheju-do violence continued, with the constabulary commander murdered on 18 June.
The Constitution passed 12 July, Rhee Syngman was elected President by 180 votes on 20 July, and the Republic of Korea was proclaimed 15 August 1948, ending USAMGIK.
By end-July 85 percent of Japanese-owned farmland had been sold to tenants through the National Land Administration, and about 494,699 farms had been sold by June.
SKIG closed with an overdraft of about 22,500 million won, while the Office of Property Custody administered roughly 85,000 million won of vested property.
No. 35 reports summer grain collection of 107,766 tons and padded ration rolls neared 9,987,000, raising suspicion of ghost recipients, as economic offices passed to Korean ministries.

sections.title: Front matter (Google Books notice)
sections.summary: Google Books digitization notice, a library-stamp image and pages marked only "Digitized by Google"; no report content.

sections.title: No. 33 (June 1948): Front matter
sections.summary: Cover of South Korean Interim Government Activities No. 33, June 1948, prepared by the National Economic Board; map of Korea, 1 July 1948 organization charts, 30 June Board roster (Acting Chairman C. H. Donnelly) and contents.

sections.title: No. 33: Summary
sections.summary: Monsoon rains quieted Cheju and southern disorders, but the North Korean power cutoff cut output from April (flour down 33 percent, paper 57). Wholesale prices stood 12-fold above 1945; over 15,000 refugees crossed the parallel.

sections.title: No. 33, Part I: Basic Aspects
sections.summary: Over 15,000 refugees crossed the 38th parallel in June; seven Kobe and Osaka school-closure rioters were jailed in Japan; the Office of Property Custody processed 69,223,437 won in capital requests and decided 141 title claims.

sections.title: Population and Foreign Affairs
sections.summary: Over 15,000 refugees crossed the 38th parallel in June; cumulative movement was 886,385 outbound and 2,424,175 inbound. In Japan, a Korean trade association formed and seven Kobe and Osaka school-closure rioters were jailed by a Hyogo military court.

sections.title: Vested Property
sections.summary: The Office of Property Custody collected 3,370 financial statements, processed 69,223,437 won in capital requests and surveyed 3,072 former Japanese corporations. It took over the Korean Residence Management Corporation and decided 141 title claims.

sections.title: No. 33, Part II: Production and Supply
sections.summary: Summer grain planted on 1,889,606 acres; first weighted wholesale index shows prices twelve-fold since 1945; the power cutoff cut flour, cotton and cement output; imports of 368 million won against exports of 323 million; Pusan stevedore reforms.

sections.title: Agriculture, Forestry and Fisheries
sections.summary: Summer grain was planted on 1,889,606 acres, about 15 percent lost to drought; rice transplanting ran two weeks early. NLA had sold farms to tenants (494,699 farms, 84 percent); silk cocoon credit was 1,170,368,400 won.

sections.title: Prices
sections.summary: June wholesale and retail prices rose, rice about 25 percent above May (cleaned rice 1,850 won per mal against 1,460). A supplement introduces Arthur Peterson's first weighted wholesale index, showing a twelve-fold rise since August 1945.

sections.title: Monthly wholesale, retail and controlled prices
sections.summary: Seoul retail prices rose in June, led by rice and red beans (cleaned rice 1,850 won per mal against 1,460 in May), while fish and vegetables eased. Tables cover wholesale, retail, open-market and controlled prices.

sections.title: Index Numbers of Wholesale Prices in South Korea, August 1945 to July 1948
sections.summary: Arthur G. Peterson's first weighted wholesale index (1947=100, 34 commodities) shows prices twelve-fold since August 1945, reaching 171 in July 1948. It justifies the 1947 base and gives weights and monthly group tables.

sections.title: Industrial Production
sections.summary: The northern power cutoff held down output all June. Flour rose to 1,653 tons from 1,023, but noodles fell 24.5 percent and cotton yarn 28 percent; cement idle, carbide stopped; cut tobacco hit a postwar high of 729.4 tons.

sections.title: Mining and Minerals
sections.summary: Anthracite output fell to 54,954 tons in May from 68,612 in April; bituminous imports from Japan fell to 45,729 tons in June, 25 percent below May. About 4,600 tons of U.S. pitch arrived; silver output hit an occupation high.

sections.title: Allocations and Distribution
sections.summary: The National Consumer Goods Office planned 500 million won of incentive goods for the summer grain collection. The Allocation Board approved 118.9 million won of civilian supplies and 458.2 million won of Korean goods; 6,360 tons of salt were distributed.

sections.title: Imports and Exports
sections.summary: June licenses showed exports of about 323 million won against imports of 368 million. Oh Chung-soo and John Thorn attended the ECAFE session in India; the FLC credit expired 30 June with $2,139,775 committed.

sections.title: Labor
sections.summary: Pusan stevedore dispute eased: contractors cut from 24 to eight, tonnage split moved from 80-20 to 70-30, and a hiring hall replaced the honcho system on 27 June. Child labor violations were found in 94 percent of Seoul firms inspected.

sections.title: No. 33, Part III: Public Services
sections.summary: Railroads carried 3,069,000 passengers against 4,298,000 in May; only 41 million KWH of power reached consumers; 133 fires cost 353 million won; Waegwan Bridge deck began 19 June; communications staff fell for a fifth month.

sections.title: Transportation
sections.summary: Revenue was about 14 percent below May; expenditures rose to 554,289,000 won. Railroads carried 3,069,000 passengers against 4,298,000 in May and about 440,564 tons of freight; operable locomotives stayed at 247 of 656.

sections.title: Communications
sections.summary: Revenue rose nearly 20 million won in June, led by telephone income; staff fell for a fifth straight month under a reduction-in-force order. Postal savings deposits stood at 846 million won; insurance policies fell 38.5 percent.

sections.title: Public Utilities
sections.summary: Only 41 million KWH reached consumers in June, down 15 million from May, the first full month without northern power. U.S. Army engineers began investigating on 28 June; 136 Seoul streetcars ran.

sections.title: Public Works
sections.summary: First-quarter road subsidies of 50,222 thousand won (of 201,888 total) went to provinces; 11 national bridge projects stood at 30 June. The Masan-Chinhae tunnel opened; 133 fires cost 353 million won.

sections.title: No. 33, Part IV: Finance
sections.summary: Bank of Chosun notes reached 30,000 million won; SKIG overdraft stood at 21,268 million. May deposits hit a record 58,280 million won, while loans outstanding fell 696 million to 29,328 million.

sections.title: Government Finance
sections.summary: Bank of Chosun notes rose from 28,200 million won in April to 30,000 million at end-June. Cumulative SKIG overdraft stood at 21,268 million; May revenue was 1,736 million against expenditure of 1,644 million.

sections.title: Non-Government Finance
sections.summary: May deposits reached a record 58,280 million won, with government balances at 34,315 million. Loans outstanding fell 696 million to 29,328 million; Yun Ho-byung became Bank of Chosun governor.

sections.title: No. 33, Part V: Government and Politics
sections.summary: The Assembly adopted its rules 153 to 1 and began the Constitution; June police work was far quieter than May, with two policemen killed; Cheju constabulary commander murdered 18 June; 22,331 prisoners held in 19 prisons.

sections.title: Administration
sections.summary: The Korea Civil Service processed 1,719 appointments and 1,979 resignations in June. The National Economic Board met five times, approving Transportation's 7,644 million won budget; USAMGIK personnel totaled 3,178.

sections.title: Political Developments
sections.summary: The National Assembly adopted its rules 153 to 1, formed nine standing committees and a Constitution drafting committee. First reading of the Constitution ended 30 June amid dispute over presidential powers and unicameralism.

sections.title: Legal Affairs
sections.summary: Executive Order 22 indefinitely postponed the Cheju-do by-election; Order 23 created an Election Review Board. The 19 prisons held 22,331 prisoners, and Chonju clerks were arrested for leftism.

sections.title: National Police
sections.summary: June was far quieter than May: two policemen killed against over 30 in May. On Cheju-do the constabulary commander was murdered 18 June and about 3,000 rioters were reported arrested.

sections.title: Inter-Zone Activities
sections.summary: Over 41,500 pieces of mail were exchanged at Tosong in four weekly exchanges, 65 percent southbound. Radio Pyongyang denounced the South Korean election, and North Korea announced price cuts on 280 items.

sections.title: No. 33, Part VI: Social (printed as Part IV)
sections.summary: Public health nursing course began with 13 nurses; 38,816 homeless families; teacher summer sessions for about 7,520 teachers; Korean National Youth reached 873,310 members; women made up 300 of 3,250 registered doctors.

sections.title: Public Health and Welfare
sections.summary: A public health nursing course began with 13 nurses and about 100 were recruited for the Constabulary Nurses Corps. About 6,100 Mukden refugees were processed at Inchon; 38,816 homeless families faced a 5,476-unit housing plan.

sections.title: Education
sections.summary: Summer sessions (26 July to 21 August) were planned to train about 7,520 teachers in 18 localities with 3,384,000 won in subsidies. Textbook distribution since 1945 totaled 14,567,626.

sections.title: Press and Public Opinion
sections.summary: Press focused on the National Assembly's opening and the 23 June draft constitution, the 8 June Dok Do bombing, the power cutoff and false reports of Japanese officials in Korea, which Hodge and Dean denied.

sections.title: Korean National Youth, Inc.
sections.summary: Korean National Youth grew to 873,310 members, a June gain of only 14,087 from tighter screening. It trained 10,573 reserve leaders and ran 981 literacy classes and 159 speakers' bureaus.

sections.title: Women's Activities
sections.summary: Women made up 300 of 3,250 registered doctors; Women's Medical University (404 students) was certified as a college in June. Covers the Nurses' Association (1,000 members), KNY women (114,370) and a home economics radio program.

sections.title: No. 34 (July-August 1948): Front matter
sections.summary: Front matter of No. 34 (July-August 1948), the final SKIG report: cover, board members, staff credits, Arthur Peterson's foreword on the Republic's founding 15 August, and table of contents.

sections.title: No. 34: Summary
sections.summary: Chairman Anderson's summary of three years of USAMGIK rule ending 15 August 1948: 1,250,000 net population influx, private trade gap cut from 400 to 25 per cent, 85,000 million won of vested property, 22,000 million won overdraft.

sections.title: No. 34, Part I: Basic Aspects
sections.summary: Net population inflow of 1,567,862 against 886,618 outbound; 151 Turk-Tartars emigrated to Turkey; Office of Property Custody investigated 5,358 companies, installed boards at 35 and handled USAFIK property releases.

sections.title: Population and Foreign Affairs
sections.summary: Net inflow of 1,567,862 against 886,618 outbound; 185,441 refugees came from the north in 1946 and 163,253 in 1947. 151 stateless Turk-Tartars emigrated to Turkey; natural increase was 3.1 per cent.

sections.title: Vested Property
sections.summary: Background of Ordinance Nos. 2 and 33, Office of Property Custody reorganization before handover, and sharply higher sales. Memorandum 32 covered Allied property; 5,358 companies were investigated and 35 boards installed.

sections.title: No. 34, Part II: Production and Supply
sections.summary: Crop near 6,000,000 metric tons; Seoul wholesale prices at 184 percent of 1947 in August; Peterson-era trade statistics (imports 3.64 billion won January-July); about 118,000 union members; the Wage Stabilization Division of 25 March 1948.

sections.title: Food and Agriculture
sections.summary: The 1948 crop is estimated near 6,000,000 metric tons, highest since 1941; summer grain collection reached 95.8 percent of quota. Ration rolls passed 9,400,000; the 7 July typhoon flooded about 504,500 acres.

sections.title: Prices
sections.summary: Seoul wholesale prices rose to 184 percent of the 1947 average in August, against 171 in July. A new weighted urban retail index from 32 series in nine cities reached 179 in August.

sections.title: Industrial Production
sections.summary: Power loss since the 14 May cutoff curbed July and August production: flour, paper, cement and brick fell. Tobacco output set a post-liberation peak in August; salt fell to 4,808 tons in July.

sections.title: Mining and Minerals
sections.summary: Anthracite output at government-financed mines fell to about 39,000 tons in July from 69,000 in April, with Samchuk and Hwasun hit hardest. Bituminous imports from Japan were 104,055 tons in July and 97,864 in August.

sections.title: Allocations and Distribution
sections.summary: The National Consumer Goods Office, created by Executive Order 12, had processed 1,095 allocations worth 2,184 million won by 31 August. Barter trade with North Korea totaled 950.9 million won.

sections.title: Imports and Exports
sections.summary: Reviews trade since 1945 (barter only, licensing, 10 per cent tariff). January-July 1948 imports were 3.64 billion won against exports of 2.76 billion; August licenses implied 722 million against 361 million.

sections.title: Summary
sections.summary: Traces foreign trade from barter-only 1945 to the 1948 licensing system: customs cut to 10 per cent in October 1946, Foreign Commerce Regulation No. 1 of July 1946, new procedures of 25 August 1947.

sections.title: Private Trade Statistics
sections.summary: Private imports were 168 million won in 1946, over 2 billion in 1947 and 3.64 billion January-July 1948, against exports of 2.76 billion. August permits implied imports of 722 million and exports of 361 million won.

sections.title: Private Trade Activities
sections.summary: Six commercial shipping companies had agents in South Korea; the Hong Kong-Pusan rate was HK$65 per ton; 15 businessmen were cleared in August. First Korean merchant cargo to Hong Kong, March 1948, was worth 123 million won.

sections.title: Government-to-Government Transactions
sections.summary: The Bureau of Foreign Commerce was sole government negotiator: trade with Japan ($828,457 July to 15 August), the US, Hong Kong (agar agar, ginseng) and China. The Pusan office handled 15,141 tons of government cargo.

sections.title: Korean Items for Americans in Korea
sections.summary: Since 1 August 1947 the Army Exchange Service has bought Korean goods through the Bureau of Foreign Commerce; by 15 August 1948, 160,789 units worth $223,063 sold, falling to $4,857 in July.

sections.title: Civilian Supply Imports
sections.summary: Total civilian supply imports were $328,117,607 to 30 June 1948, including $24,935,669 through FLC. Coal from Japan reached a record 104,055 tons in July; over 500,000 tons of fertilizer and $14.8 million of petroleum imported.

sections.title: Labor
sections.summary: About 118,000 union members, mostly in the rightist Tai Han, with communist Chun Pyung driven underground. Wage policy ended in the 25 March 1948 Wage Stabilization Division; July-August items include the Fusan stevedore wage dispute.

sections.title: No. 34, Part III: Public Services
sections.summary: 268 operable locomotives in August; July communications revenue highest since liberation; 56.2 and 55.7 million KWH delivered in July and August; Giroux Power Mission's 23 July recommendations; 517 bridges and 1,422 km of road restored.

sections.title: Transportation
sections.summary: August income was the highest since liberation, with rail receipts 15 per cent above July. Covers 268 operable locomotives in August 1948, Rainbow Service ships and LSTs, and the Korean Truck Company.

sections.title: Communications
sections.summary: July 1948 revenue was the highest since liberation, helped by the 1 June rate rise, while expenditure more than doubled. Employment fell 7,468 since November 1946; 37,183 telephones, 623 post offices and 11 radio stations.

sections.title: Public Utilities
sections.summary: Deliveries were 56.2 and 55.7 million KWH in July and August after the 14 May northern cut-off. Chung Pyung transformer repaired 10 July; the Giroux Power Mission made recommendations 23 July; 137 Seoul streetcars ran.

sections.title: Public Works
sections.summary: Public Works restored 517 bridges and 1,422 km of road since 1946. June flood bridge losses were 28.47 million won; the Emergency Water Conservation Board formed 28 July; 1,006 fires occurred January-June.

sections.title: No. 34, Part IV: Finance
sections.summary: Bank of Chosun notes about 30,000 million won and overdraft of 22,506 million at 31 August; August revenue 2,157 million. Deposits of 43,335 million won; 30,038 million of loans outstanding.

sections.title: Government Finance
sections.summary: Bank of Chosun notes were about 30,000 million won on 31 August, with an overdraft of 22,506 million. FY 1948/49 appropriations reached 29,004 million; August revenue was 2,157 million against spending of 1,924 million.

sections.title: Non-Government Finance
sections.summary: Deposits were 43,335 million won (33 per cent government), with cash balances of 2,244 million and 30,038 million of loans outstanding after record new loans. Life insurance in force passed 1,067 million.

sections.title: No. 34, Part V: Government and Politics
sections.summary: Republic proclaimed 15 August; Constitution passed 12 July; Rhee elected President by 180 votes 20 July; Lee Bum-suk approved as Prime Minister 110 to 84; police arrests over the 25 August North Korean election; 22,321 prisoners.

sections.title: Administration
sections.summary: The Republic was proclaimed 15 August 1948, ending Military Government; the Civil Affairs Section of USAFIK succeeded it. The Economic Board raised the rice price to 150 won; personnel fell to 2,870.

sections.title: Political Developments
sections.summary: The Constitution passed 12 July; Rhee Syngman was elected President by 180 votes on 20 July with Lee Si-young Vice-President. Lee Bum-suk was approved as Prime Minister 110 to 84.

sections.title: Legal Affairs
sections.summary: Ordinances Nos. 203-219 and legal opinions on repatriate pensions, the Mining Development Corporation and the metric system. Prison population was 22,321 in July; the Guards Training School graduated 174.

sections.title: National Police
sections.summary: Communists forced South Koreans to sign endorsements of the 25 August North Korean election, with arrests in Pusan, Chungchong, Cholla and Taegu (200 held). Detective Bureau chiefs resigned after a torture-death case; Yun Chie-yung became Internal Affairs Minister.

sections.title: Inter-Zone Activities
sections.summary: Mail exchange moved to weekly meetings at Tosong from 15 April 1948. Commerce Order No. 4 (effective 2 August) required permits for overland barter; an American soldier was killed 19 July at the parallel.

sections.title: No. 34, Part VI: Social
sections.summary: Floods and typhoons made about 254,664 persons needy; 7,500 teachers attended summer workshops; Ordinances 215-217 effective 12 August; Korean National Youth reached 1,154,821 members; 500 policewomen; Korea placed 24th at the London Olympics.

sections.title: Public Health and Welfare
sections.summary: Floods and typhoons washed away 3,604 houses and made about 254,664 persons needy; hog cholera hit five provinces (15,291 dead). 8,616 Manchurian repatriates arrived; cholera deaths fell from over 15,000 to 10.

sections.title: Education
sections.summary: Ordinances 215, 216 and 217, effective 12 August, created county school districts, nine-member elected school boards and local school taxation. About 7,500 teachers attended workshops; 14,989,286 textbooks printed since liberation.

sections.title: Press and Public Opinion
sections.summary: Newspapers focused on forming the new government: the Assembly's 108-88 vote putting police under Internal Affairs, rejection of Lee Yun-yung, approval of Lee Bum-suk as Premier. They protested the North Korean election and reported floods costing 2,000 million won.

sections.title: Korean National Youth, Inc.
sections.summary: Korean National Youth, chartered 9 October 1945, reached 1,154,821 audited members by 15 August 1948. It donated over 12.6 million work days, planted 6,770,397 trees and trained over 100,000 group leaders.

sections.title: Women's Activities
sections.summary: The Constitution and military ordinances guarantee women equality; 500 policewomen serve. Louise Yim became Minister of Commerce and Industry and Helen Kim UN delegation secretary; Ordinance 70 bans sale of women.

sections.title: Culture
sections.summary: Hangul was reintroduced in October 1945; a dictionary was printed. The American Language Institute has about 500 students. Korea competed under its own flag at the London Olympics (30 July-15 August), scoring 15 points and placing 24th.

sections.title: No. 35 (September-October 1948): Front matter
sections.summary: Cover and front matter of Republic of Korea Economic Summation No. 35 (September-October 1948), prepared by Civil Affairs Section, USAFIK. Foreword says political and social sections are dropped and No. 36 will run to 31 December 1948.

sections.title: No. 35: Summary
sections.summary: Summer grain purchase reached 107,766 tons (100.4 percent of goal); rice goal set at 1,125,000 tons; ghost ration recipients suspected. Power fell 18 percent, wholesale prices stood at 177 percent of 1947, and property sales totaled 2,601 million won.

sections.title: No. 35, Part I: Basic Aspects
sections.summary: Refugee crossings were 11,718 in September and 7,764 in October; net immigration since October 1945 added 1,588,030 people. Property custody passed to Korean custodians by 12 October; cumulative sales reached 2,611 million won.

sections.title: Population
sections.summary: Refugee crossings of the 38th parallel were 11,718 in September (up 57 percent) and 7,764 in October (down 33 percent). Net immigration since October 1945 was 1,588,030: outbound 887,301, inbound 2,475,331.

sections.title: Vested Property
sections.summary: Transfer to Korean custodians was completed by 12 October; US staff fell from 96 to 58. Sales of immovables and vested shares stopped 18 September; cumulative sales were 2,611 million won; 825 of 1,394 claims allowed.

sections.title: No. 35, Part II: Production and Supply
sections.summary: Summer grain collection 107,766 tons; rice quota of 1,125,000 tons; wholesale prices at 177 percent of 1947; imports rose 118 percent in August; Hong Kong took over 93 percent of exports; anthracite down 51 percent from April.

sections.title: Food and Agriculture
sections.summary: Administration passed to the Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry on 13 September. Summer grain collection closed at 107,766 tons against 100,217 in 1947; the rice quota was 1,125,000 tons; ration rolls neared 9,987,000.

sections.title: Prices
sections.summary: Wholesale prices fell in October to 177 percent of the 1947 average from 184 in August, with grains and protein foods declining while textiles and fuels climbed. The Bureau of Prices set no new controlled prices.

sections.title: Industrial Production
sections.summary: Output improved slightly despite power shortages. Flour and noodles hit 1948 highs in September; briquettes reached 15,849 tons and oxygen 99,000 cubic meters. No carbide was made and cement stopped in November for lack of power.

sections.title: Mining and Minerals
sections.summary: Anthracite output fell for the fifth straight month in September, 51 percent below April; the 70,500-ton quota proved unrealistic. Bituminous imports from Japan totaled 100,015 tons in September, falling 10 percent in October.

sections.title: Allocations and Distribution
sections.summary: On 16 August the Allocations Bureau of the new Office of Planning replaced the consumer goods bodies; by October it had processed 1,211 allocations worth 2,551,813,628 won. Salt distribution was 37,181 tons.

sections.title: Imports and Exports
sections.summary: Imports rose 118 percent in August over July while exports fell 18 percent; in September imports rose 22 percent and exports over 80 percent. Private imports were 1,155 million won; Hong Kong took over 93 percent of exports.

sections.title: No. 35, Part III: Public Services
sections.summary: Transportation and Communications passed to the Republic in August-September; electricity distribution was 45.6 and 46.1 million KWH; Yongwol tested at 80,400 KW on 23 October; Public Works became a bureau 13 September.

sections.title: Transportation
sections.summary: Transportation passed to the Republic on 15 August under Minister Min He-sik, who resigned 6 October in favor of Ho Chung. September income rose almost 12 percent but expenditures jumped 61 percent to a record.

sections.title: Communications
sections.summary: Communications passed to the Republic on 13 September under Minister Yoon Suk-ku. Employment stood at 12,570; postal depositors rose 153,000, and spending hit a post-liberation record.

sections.title: Public Utilities
sections.summary: Distribution was 45.6 million KWH in September and 46.1 million in October, about 18 percent below August. Yongwol tested at 80,400 KW on 23 October; a seven-man Korean Power Mission under Loyal Millburn arrived 19 October.

sections.title: Public Works
sections.summary: On 13 September Public Works became a bureau under the Ministry of Home Affairs. Highway work totaled 82,677 man-days costing 41,336 thousand won; eight bridges were under construction.

sections.title: No. 35, Part IV: Finance
sections.summary: Bank of Chosun notes rose 2,500 million won from August to October; the 1948/49 budget reached 43,749 million won. Deposits stood at 52,328 million won and loans outstanding fell to 27,441 million.

sections.title: Government Finance
sections.summary: Bank of Chosun notes outstanding rose 2,500 million won from August to October, partly from 1,500 million for leaf tobacco. Spending exceeded revenue by 3,695 million in September; the 1948/49 budget reached 43,749 million won.

sections.title: Non-Government Finance
sections.summary: Cash balances reached 4,691.9 million won in September. Total deposits were 52,328 million won, 38 per cent government. Loans outstanding fell 960 million won to 27,441 million.

sections.title: Back matter
sections.summary: Back matter with no report content: blank digitized pages, a library date-due slip stamped June 2010, and a closing Google Books page.
